To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Helicobacter‐associated chronic gastritis is a very frequent condition, and is often associated with peptic ulceration; 2) Non‐steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are associated with chronic gastritis, but only in the presence of Helicobacter; and 3) Non‐steroidals do not cause gastritis in Helicobacter-negative patients.

(1) H pylori infection is the most common cause of histological gastritis; (2) H pylori gastritis is associated with a high risk of peptic ulceration; (3) H pylori‐induced gastritis is associated in some patients with a high risk for gastric carcinoma; and (4) non‐steroidal ant‐inflammatory drugs may cause gastritis in H pylori‐infected individuals but not in those without H pylori.

the prevalence of Helicobacter associated chronic gastritis is significantly increased by long‐term use of non‐steroidal drugs, but that this is not the case with acute or short‐term non‐steroidal drug use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Helicobacter infection in the pathogenesis of chronic gastritis in patients taking nonsteroidal anti‐ inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
the role of Helicobacter in peptic ulcer disease, the development of new diagnostic methods and the development of new therapeutic approaches.

the role of Helicobacter in the pathogenesis of chronic gastritis, peptic ulceration, and gastric cancer, with the aim of identifying those patients at risk of complications of infection and developing new approaches to the prevention and treatment of Helicobacterspecific disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

H. pylori is a common cause of chronic gastritis, that NSAID therapy may exacerbate H. pylori gastritis, but that the evidence that NSAIDs are the commonest cause of gastritis in patients with peptic ulceration is weak.

NSAID‐associated gastritis and duodenitis are not common, and are not associated with peptic ulceration, but are a rare cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers in patients who are infected with Helicobacter.

the prevalence of Helicobacter infection in patients taking nonsteroidal anti‐ inflammatory drugs is not significantly different from the prevalence of Helcobacter infection in the general population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
non‐steroidals do cause chronic gastritis, but that the majority of cases are not associated with H. pylori.
the prevalence of H pylori infection in patients with chronic gastritis is similar to that in patients with duodenal ulcers, and is significantly higher than in those with peptic gastric ulcers.
the association between non‐steroidal drugs and chronic gastritis is real but not as great as was previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NSAIDs are a major cause of peptic ulceration, and that this is a common complication of chronic NSAID use.
the prevalence of H. pylori infection in patients with NSAID‐associated gastritis is similar to that of the general population and that NSAID use alone is not a risk factor for H. pylori acquisition.
H. pylori is an independent risk factor for the development of gastric cancer, and that eradication of the infection is associated with a reduced incidence of gastric cancer.
